title: Context and Memory: How an Agent Handles Long Tasks

lines.en: Welcome back. Last time, we opened up an AI agent and looked {inside}inside.
We saw that the model {only}only reads text and {writes}writes text. On its own, it can't {open}open a file or run a command.
The {harness}harness runs the loop. When the model asks for a tool, the harness {executes}executes it and {adds}adds the result to the conversation.
That conversation is a {list}list of messages. And on {every}every call, the harness sends the {whole}whole list to the model again.
All of it has to fit inside the {cw}context window, which is {limited}limited.
We called it the model's {desk}desk. And that desk has a {fixed}fixed size.

lines.topic: Hook: the context window fills up
lines.en: But real tasks are {long}long. An agent might need {hundreds}hundreds of steps to finish one job.
Watch. {c5}Call five. {c20}Call twenty. {c60}Call sixty. Every step {adds}adds more messages.
The meter {climbs}climbs. {amber}Amber. {red}Red. And then the window is {full}full.
The task isn't {finished}finished. The desk is {full}full. {now}Now what?
How do real agents {keep}keep working? And how do they {remember}remember things from yesterday?
That's today's lesson: {title}context and memory.

chapter.title: What Is Actually Filling the Context?

lines.en: So first, what is {actually}actually filling the context window?
At the top is the {system}system message. {small}Small, and always there.
Then the {tools}tool descriptions. Also {small}small, and always present.
{user}User messages are usually thin, like a short question. The {assistant}assistant's messages and tool calls are {thin}thin too.
But {tool}tool results can be very {tall}tall.
The model {requests}requests read_file, on a {large}large file.
The harness {adds}adds the result as one tool message, and the meter {jumps}jumps from 20% to 60% in one step.
{sort}Sort everything by type, and the picture is clear. In many agent tasks, {most}tool results take the most space.
And {remember}remember: everything in the window is {sent}sent again on {every}every call.
lines.topic: Everything is sent again on every call

lines.en: So one large tool result is {paid}paid for again and again, in {time}time and in {cost}cost.

chapter.title: Why Not Just Use a Bigger Window?

lines.en: So why not just make the window {bigger}bigger?
Bigger windows {help}help, but they don't {solve}solve the problem. Here's why.
{one}One: it still has a limit. A long enough task {fills}fills even a big window.
{two}Two: it gets {slower}slower and more {expensive}expensive. More text in every call means each call {costs}costs more and takes longer.

{three}Three: important details get {harder}harder to find. When the context is very long and {cluttered}cluttered, models often become less {reliable}reliable at using the right piece of information.
lines.topic: Details get lost in long contexts

lines.en: Like the user's original {goal}goal: still in there, but {lost}lost among hundreds of other messages.
A bigger {desk}desk covered with a thousand papers doesn't help you work. A {clean}clean desk with the {right}right ten papers does.
This is called {cm}context management: deciding what the model {sees}sees on each call. It's the {harness}harness's job, set up by the developers who build it.
The goal is not {more}more context. The goal is the {right}right context.
{tech}Technique one: keep tool results {small}small.
The {cheapest}cheapest way to save space is to {not}not put unnecessary text into the context in the first place.
{first}First, read only the {part}part you need.
{before}Before: read_file returns a {whole}whole five-thousand-line file.
{after}After: the tool call asks only for {lines}lines 40 to 80, and a {small}small card comes back.
{second}Second, {search}search instead of reading everything.
{before}Before: the agent reads {ten}ten files to find where total() is. {after}After: one {search}search returns three short {matching}matching lines.
{third}Third, the harness {shortens}shortens very long output.
A run_command result can be {thousands}thousands of lines. The harness keeps the {beginning}beginning and the {end}end, with a {note}note in the middle: output shortened, 4,800 more lines.
That note {matters}matters. The harness must {tell}tell the model that text was cut.
{without}Without it, the model thinks it has seen {everything}everything, and answers {confidently}confidently from a wrong assumption.
{with}With the note, the model knows something is {missing}missing, and {asks}asks for the part it needs.
{tech}Technique two: {trim}trim old messages.
When the window gets {full}full, the harness {removes}removes the oldest messages so new ones fit.
Here the window is at {pct}95%, and a {new}new message needs to come in.
The {oldest}oldest messages slide out, the {drops}meter drops, and the new one {fits}fits.

lines.topic: System message pinned, tool calls leave in pairs
lines.en: The {system}system message stays {pinned}pinned at the top. And a tool call and its result always leave {together}together, as a {pair}pair.
A {gentler}gentler version empties only old, large {tool}tool results, and leaves a {note}short note in their place.
But trimming has a {danger}danger. The {first}first user message said: Fix the crash. Do not change the {public}public function names.
That message gets {trimmed}trimmed away. A few steps {later}later, the model {renames}renames a function. It can {no}no longer see the instruction.
Trimming is {simple}simple and fast, but it's {blind}blind. It throws away old messages, {important}important or not.
And once a message is {out}out of the window, the model {cannot}cannot see it any more.
{tech}Technique three: {summarize}summarize old messages.
Instead of {throwing}throwing old messages away, the harness {replaces}replaces them with a short {summary}summary. This is commonly called {compaction}compaction.
{step}Step one: the harness {notices}notices the window is getting full. The meter crosses a {threshold}threshold, in this example {pct}80%.
{step}Step two: the harness makes a {separate}separate call to the model, with the {older}older messages and one {instruction}instruction: Summarize the important points of this conversation so far.
{step}Step three: the model {writes}writes the summary, as normal text. The harness only decides {when}when to ask, and {what}what to replace.
{step}Step four: the harness {swaps}swaps them. The older messages {become}become one summary. The {system}system message stays on top, and the {newest}newest messages stay as they are.
{step}Step five: the meter {drops}drops to 25%, and the loop {continues}continues.
A good summary keeps the {goal}goal, the user's {rules}rules, what's {done}done, what's {left}left, and key {facts}facts like file names and errors.
But a summary is {lossy}lossy. An old message said: the user wants error messages in {simple}simple words.
The summary {left}left it out. So the model never {sees}sees it again, and stops {following}following it.
{comparing}Comparing the three: {small}small tool results save space {early}early, but you might {miss}miss a part you needed.
{trimming}Trimming saves {lot}a lot, but can lose old {instructions}instructions completely.
{summarizing}Summarizing saves a lot too, but can lose small {details}details.
Every technique for saving space {loses}loses something. Context management is {choosing}choosing what you can afford to lose.
All of this happens inside {one}one conversation. What about {tomorrow}tomorrow?
A {session}session is one continuous conversation with the agent, from {start}start to {end}end.
In session {one}one, Rahul says: In this project, {always}always run the tests before you say a task is done. The agent {follows}follows it.
Then the session {ends}ends, and the context window is {cleared}cleared.
In session {two}two, the agent {skips}skips the tests. The rule is {gone}gone, because the message that held it is gone.

lines.topic: Memory: a notebook outside the window
lines.en: {memory}Memory is information the harness saves {outside}outside the context window, usually in {files}ordinary files, so it can be {back}brought back later.
The context window is the {desk}desk. Memory is a {notebook}notebook in the drawer. The desk gets {cleared}cleared every day. The notebook {stays}stays.
Now, session one {again}again, with memory. Rahul adds: {remember}Remember this.
The model replies with a {call}tool call to {save}save_note, with the text: Always run tests before finishing a task.
The harness {executes}executes it. It {saves}saves the note in the notebook, and adds a {tool}tool message: Note saved.
The session {ends}ends. The messages are gone, but the notebook {keeps}keeps its note.
In session {two}two, before the {first}first call, the harness {puts}puts the saved notes into the context window.
Rahul says: {fix}Fix the login bug.
The model {fixes}fixes it, and before {reporting}reporting back, it calls {run}run_command to run the tests.
It's exactly the {same}same model in both sessions. It didn't {learn}learn anything.
It follows the rule only because the harness put the {note}note back into the {text}text it received.
The model doesn't {remember}remember. The harness {writes}writes it down and {brings}brings it back.
Worth saving: {facts}facts, like how the tests are run. {rules}Rules, like: do not rename public functions.
And {progress}progress, like: login bug, cause found, fix not written yet.
Weeks {pass}pass, and the notebook now holds {count}300 notes.
If the harness loads them {all}all at the start of a session, the window is at {pct}70% before the user says a word.
Memory can {overflow}overflow the context too.
The answer is {retrieval}retrieval: fetching only the notes that are {relevant}relevant to the current task.
A few short core rules are {always}always loaded, at the start of every session. {else}Everything else stays in the notebook until it's {needed}needed.
Rahul says: {deploy}Deploy the app to the test server.
The model replies with a {call}tool call to {search}search_notes, with the query: {query}deploy.
The harness {searches}searches the notebook. Out of {n300}300 notes, {two}2 match.
It adds a {tool}tool message with just those two notes, and the meter has {barely}barely moved.
It's the {same}same tool-calling pattern as before. The model {requests}requests, the harness {does}does. Memory is just {another}another tool, plus a {place}place to store text.
There are {smarter}smarter ways to search notes than matching words. We'll meet those in a {later}later lesson.
Now let's put it all {together}together: one long task, across {two}two sessions.
Session {one}one. Rahul says: {fix}Fix all failing tests in this project. Don't rename public functions.
The model calls {run}run_command to run the tests. The output is very {long}long, so the harness {shortens}shortens it. That's technique {one}one.
Then {read}read_file, for lines 40 to 80 only. Technique one {again}again.
Then {edit}edit_file, and the file is {updated}updated.
The work goes {on}on, call after call. By call forty, the meter is at {pct}80%.
{compaction}Compaction kicks in. That's technique {three}three. The older messages become one {summary}summary, and the meter {drops}drops to 25%.
The model finds out why the login tests {fail}fail, and calls {save}save_note: Login tests fail because of a wrong port in config.txt.
Rahul says: Let's {stop}stop for today. One more {save}save_note, with the {progress}progress: 6 of 8 tests pass. {next}Next: fix the port, then run tests.
The session {ends}ends. The notebook {keeps}keeps its notes.
Session {two}two. The harness {loads}loads the notes. The meter is at just {pct}5%.
Rahul says: {continue}Continue from yesterday.
The model calls {read}read_file on config.txt. The result: {port}port = 8800. That's the {wrong}wrong port.
Then {edit}edit_file to fix the port, and {run}run_command to run the tests. All 8 tests {passed}passed.
And a final {answer}answer, with no tool call: All tests pass now. The last two failed because config.txt had the {wrong}wrong port. No public {functions}functions were renamed.
Two things {survived}survived. The {rule}rule survived compaction, because the {summary}summary kept it.
And the {progress}progress survived the end of the session, because it was saved to {memory}memory.

chapter.title: Reality Check: Memory Can Be Wrong

lines.topic: Reality check: memory can be wrong
lines.en: A {reality}reality check before we finish. Memory is useful, but it isn't {magic}magic.
{one}One: summaries lose {details}details. What a summary leaves out is {gone}gone.
{two}Two: notes can be out of {date}date. A note says the server port is {p8080}8080, but config.txt now says {p9090}9090. If the agent {trusts}trusts the old note, it makes a {mistake}mistake.
Good agents {check}check important facts again.
{three}Three: notes can be {wrong}wrong from the start. A wrong conclusion, once saved, gets {repeated}repeated in later sessions.
{four}Four: memory can hold {private}private information. You should be able to {see}see what is saved, and {delete}delete it.
More memory is not {automatically}automatically better. Like context, the aim is the {right}right information at the right {time}time.
Today we {solved}solved the problem from last time. The context window is {limited}limited, so the harness has to {choose}choose what the model sees.
It can keep tool results {small}small, drop old messages, or replace them with a {summary}summary.
And for anything that must {last}last longer than one conversation, it writes it down in {memory}memory, and brings it back when it's needed.
Remember the most {important}important point. The model itself {never}never remembers anything. It only {sees}sees the text that the harness gives it.
But there is still {one}one thing we haven't looked at. So far, our agent decides just {step}one step at a time.
What happens when the goal is really {big}big, like building a whole {app}app? How does an agent {break}break a big goal into small steps, and keep {track}track of them?
That's what we'll learn in the next lesson: {planning}Planning.
